why: Il2 is the mouse ortholog of human IL2 and encodes interleukin-2, a cytokine produced mainly by activated T cells. IL-2 signals through receptors containing the IL-2 receptor alpha, beta, and gamma chains and has been associated with proliferation and regulation of T cells, including effector and regulatory T-cell populations.

IL-2-based agents are used in cancer and are under study in autoimmune disease, where high- and low-dose approaches have different effects; engineered IL-2 variants aim to bias these responses. Il2-deficient mice are viable and develop immune dysregulation, consistent with a role in immune homeostasis.
applications: Humanized IL2 models, in which the human cytokine replaces the mouse counterpart, have been used to evaluate IL-2-based agents and engineered IL-2 variants in defined experimental settings.
Il2 knockout mice have been used to study T-cell regulation and tolerance.

why: Il15 is the mouse ortholog of human IL15 and encodes interleukin-15, a cytokine that shares receptor components with IL-2 and is often presented in trans by IL-15 receptor alpha. IL-15 has been associated with the development and maintenance of natural killer cells and memory CD8 T cells.
IL-15-based agents, including IL-15 superagonists, are under study in cancer immunotherapy. Il15-deficient mice are viable and show reduced natural killer and memory T-cell populations.
applications: Humanized IL15 models, often paired with IL-15 receptor components, have been used to evaluate IL-15-based agents and to support human immune-cell functions in defined experimental settings.
Il15 knockout mice have been used to study natural killer and memory T-cell biology.

why: Cd40 is the mouse ortholog of human CD40 and encodes CD40, a TNF-receptor-superfamily member expressed on antigen-presenting cells and other cells. CD40 binds CD40 ligand (CD154) and has been associated with activation of antigen-presenting cells and support of T-cell and B-cell responses.

CD40 agonists are under study in cancer immunotherapy, and the CD40-CD40L axis is also implicated in inflammatory and vascular disease. Cd40-deficient mice are viable and show impaired antibody class switching and germinal-center responses.
applications: Humanized CD40 models, in which the human receptor replaces the mouse counterpart, have been used to evaluate agonistic CD40 antibodies in immunocompetent mice, sometimes combined with CD40L humanization.

why: Tnfrsf9 is the mouse ortholog of human TNFRSF9 and encodes 4-1BB (CD137), a costimulatory TNF-receptor-superfamily member expressed on activated T cells and other immune cells. Engagement of 4-1BB by its ligand has been associated with enhanced T-cell proliferation and survival.

4-1BB is a target of agonist antibodies and bispecific agents in cancer immunotherapy, and the 4-1BB signaling domain is used in some chimeric antigen receptors. Tnfrsf9-deficient mice are viable with altered T-cell responses in some models.

why: Cd276 is the mouse ortholog of human CD276 and encodes B7-H3, a member of the B7 family of immune-regulatory cell-surface proteins. B7-H3 has been associated with modulation of T-cell responses, though its receptor and precise roles remain under study.

B7-H3 is overexpressed on several tumors with limited expression in many normal tissues, and B7-H3-directed antibodies, antibody–drug conjugates, and CAR T cells have been evaluated; clinical results have varied. Cd276-deficient mice are viable with altered responses in some disease models.
applications: Humanized CD276 (B7-H3) models, in which the human protein replaces the mouse counterpart, have been used to evaluate B7-H3-targeted therapeutics, including antibody–drug conjugates and cell therapies, in defined experimental settings.

why: Nt5e is the mouse ortholog of human NT5E and encodes CD73, a GPI-anchored ecto-5’-nucleotidase that converts AMP to adenosine. CD73, together with CD39, has been associated with generation of extracellular adenosine and with regulation of immune responses.

why: Met is the mouse ortholog of human MET and encodes MET (c-MET), a receptor tyrosine kinase that binds hepatocyte growth factor. MET signaling has been associated with cell proliferation, survival, and migration.

MET alterations, including exon 14 skipping and amplification, have been associated with non-small cell lung cancer and other tumors, and MET inhibitors are used in selected MET-driven cancers; resistance can emerge. Homozygous Met-null mice show embryonic lethality with defects in placenta, liver, and muscle development.
applications: Humanized MET models, in which the human receptor replaces the mouse counterpart, have been used to evaluate MET-targeted antibodies and inhibitors.
Conditional Met models have been used to study MET signaling in defined experimental settings.

why: F11 is the mouse ortholog of human F11 and encodes coagulation factor XI, a serine protease zymogen of the intrinsic coagulation pathway. Activated factor XI has been associated with amplification of thrombin generation.

Factor XI has been associated with thrombosis while having a comparatively limited role in normal hemostasis, and factor XI inhibitors are under study as anticoagulants intended to reduce bleeding risk. F11-deficient mice are viable with prolonged clotting times and reduced experimental thrombosis.
applications: Humanized F11 models, in which the human protein replaces the mouse counterpart, have been used to evaluate factor XI-directed anticoagulants in defined experimental settings.

why: Dpp4 is the mouse ortholog of human DPP4 and encodes dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (CD26), a cell-surface and soluble serine exopeptidase. DPP-4 cleaves several peptides, including the incretin hormones GLP-1 and GIP, and has been associated with regulation of their activity.

DPP-4 inhibitors are used in type 2 diabetes, and DPP-4 has additional roles in immune regulation; in some species DPP-4 serves as a receptor for certain coronaviruses. Dpp4-deficient mice are viable and show altered glucose tolerance and incretin levels.
applications: Humanized DPP4 models, in which the human protein replaces the mouse counterpart, have been used to study DPP-4 biology, DPP-4-targeted agents, and human DPP-4-dependent coronavirus infection in defined experimental settings.
